solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Understanding when there's trouble also brewing?

definitions.text: Understanding when there's trouble also brewing?

parts.note: a brew is a pot of the hot drink, so brewing stands for that drink
also is a synonym of the joining word 'and'
understanding in the sense of fellow feeling is sympathy

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the comfort offered in a crisis comes with a pot on the go.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue back to front: brewing gives the first word, also the second, Understanding the last. The whole clue doubles as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names the kindly comfort, often with a cuppa, offered to someone who is upset or in difficulty.

clue.text: Working on aim of Jack to become GP?

parts.note: a jack, or jack tar, is an old name for a sailor
to get, as in 'get angry', means to become
GP can stand for general practice, a doctor's surgery

explanation.surface: A sailor apparently hopes to retrain as a family doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack is a sailor (TAR), not the bowls target; GP is read as general practice, not the doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: Shooting at a mark repeatedly to improve is exercise devoted to improving one's aim.

clue.text: Loving 'The Way to Felixstowe' on the radio

indicators.note: something heard on the radio is spoken, so these words signal a sound-alike

parts.note: the A14 trunk road runs to the port of Felixstowe in Suffolk, and its number is spoken as A one-four

explanation.surface: A romantic song title about an English port being broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Felixstowe is a container port in Suffolk, England, reached by the A14 road; said as 'A one four' it gives the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Being a great one for something is an idiom for being very keen on or fond of it.

clue.text: Busy, as Yankee gathering up refuse

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards
the run of words gathers the letters inside itself, so they sit hidden there

explanation.surface: An American is busy collecting rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathering' tucks the letters inside busY AS YANkee; 'up' reads them backwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To refuse is to deny or oppose, which is what a person who always says no does.

clue.text: The odds of surfie securing Indian title

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, are taken from the word that follows

explanation.surface: A surfer somehow holding an Indian honorific.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking letters one, three and five of surfie gives the answer; 'securing' just links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an honorific placed before the name of a respected man in India, like Mister.

clue.text: Deciding to oblige the men with time off

parts.note: to make someone do something is to oblige them
OR, other ranks, are the ordinary soldiers as opposed to officers
a break is a rest or time off work

explanation.surface: An employer forces the troops to take leave.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is military shorthand for other ranks, the men as opposed to officers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that will settle success or failure is decisive, deciding the outcome either way.

clue.text: Fashion dictates that one should run for gold?

definitions.text: that one should run for gold?

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so the next word's letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: A style rule says a runner ought to compete to win first place.
explanation.walkthrough: Fashion is a verb here, reshaping dictates. The definition recalls the old nitric acid check that showed whether metal was true gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldsmiths applied acid to a metal sample to prove it genuine; the phrase now means any decisive trial.

clue.text: Pound superior to yen, briefly: one concern of Japan

indicators.note: in a down clue, being superior means sitting above the next piece

parts.note: to pound is to strike or hit

indicators.note: briefly says the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: a yen is a longing, as is an ache
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Talk of sterling outperforming the Japanese currency for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: Yen is a longing (ACHE), not money; 'briefly' drops its last letter. A concern is a business firm.
explanation.definitionFit: The electronics maker is a Japanese company, and a concern is a business enterprise.

clue.text: Row in university squat almost leading to afters

parts.note: a college is a university or part of one

indicators.note: in says one piece sits within the other
almost says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: squat means short and stout, as does pudgy
a row is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: A quarrel in a student occupation leads up to dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' and 'in' are the indicators; squat is the adjective, stout, not a sit-in. Afters is British slang for dessert; college pudding is a steamed suet pudding with dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a traditional British steamed sponge with dried fruit, eaten as the sweet course after the main meal.

clue.text: Old-fashioned sporting arena's fencing in both kilometres and yards

indicators.note: fencing means enclosing, so one piece goes round the others

parts.note: a rink is an arena for skating or curling
taken as written
K is short for kilometres
YD is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: An old sports venue fenced in both metric and imperial measures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fencing' means enclosing, not swordplay, and the arena splits after its first letter to wrap the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal adjective means shabby, cheap or out of date, much like antiquated.

clue.text: Launch fortnightly shows in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means withdrawing backwards, so the letters are read in reverse
shows means the word displays some of its letters inside it

explanation.surface: A magazine's twice-monthly programmes being launched among pensioners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows' finds fORTNIghtly's inner letters and 'in retirement' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: An opening or introduction is how a piece of music or a talk is launched.

clue.text: Cockney considered taking tart in place of fantasies

indicators.note: taking means holding another piece inside
a Cockney traditionally drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to hold a view is to consider it so; held means considered
a flan is an open tart

explanation.surface: A Londoner thought about eating pastry in a dreamland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cockney' and 'taking' are the indicators. Cockneys are working-class Londoners famed for dropping the letter at the start of words like 'had'.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairyland, the realm of fairy folk, is an imaginary world full of fantasy.

clue.text: Sing about crush

parts.note: to perform a song is to do a number
on means about, as in a talk on a subject

explanation.surface: Perform a love song about an infatuation.
explanation.walkthrough: Crush is the verb, to defeat utterly, not a teenage infatuation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to defeat, humiliate or thoroughly damage someone, as a crushing victory does.

clue.text: Coal pit is out of sight

indicators.note: something that is out is disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mine has closed down and vanished from view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of sight' looks like one phrase, but 'is out' signals rearranging Coal pit and 'of sight' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to vision and the eyes, so it means relating to sight.

clue.text: A verse for Kinks fan

parts.note: a means each or per, as in five pounds a head

explanation.surface: A song verse written for a devotee of the 1960s rock band.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kinks were a 1960s British rock band; here kinks are sexual quirks.
explanation.definitionFit: A pervert, in slang shortened form, is someone into sexual kinks.

clue.text: A group holding party after English lecture

indicators.note: after places the following pieces behind the abbreviation
holding means containing the next piece

parts.note: a ring is a group or gang, such as a spy ring
a bash is a party

explanation.surface: A band hosting a celebration following an English class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' and 'after' are the indicators. Lecture is the noun, a long scolding, not a university talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A long tedious harangue or telling-off is informally called this in British slang.

clue.text: Army officer carries it in case, very small

indicators.note: carries means holding the next piece within

parts.note: LT is short for lieutenant
taken as written
lest means in case, for fear that

explanation.surface: A soldier holds something in a small box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carries' is the container signal; 'in case' is a conjunction meaning for fear that, not a container.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of little means the smallest of all, so tiniest or very small indeed.

clue.text: Scottish isle around which artist renovated properties

indicators.note: around which says the reworked word encloses the island
renovated means remade, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: Bute is an island in the Firth of Clyde, Scotland

explanation.surface: A painter does up houses on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'renovated' rearranges artist to ATTRIS; 'around which' places BUTE inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Qualities or characteristics of a thing are its features, and properties in that sense.

clue.text: Catch on toilet cabin raised in protest?

parts.note: to twig is to catch on, to understand suddenly
loo is British slang for toilet

explanation.surface: Someone realises the hut is really a lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: The word was coined for the twig-built shelters of 1990s road protesters in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Eco-protesters built domed shelters of woven branches at camps, shacks raised in a demonstration.

clue.text: Buzzer that's now loud?

parts.note: a buzzing insect that is now loud must once have been soft: in music P (piano) means quietly

explanation.surface: A doorbell or alarm that has become noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: In musical notation P (piano) means soft. Something now loud previously 'was P', and the insect is a buzzer.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped stinging insect is a buzzer because of the droning noise it makes in flight.

clue.text: A team after Test finished early going up in this?

definitions.text: A team after Test finished early going up in this?

indicators.note: after places the side behind the reversed test
in a down clue, going up means reading the letters bottom to top
finished early means the word stops short of its last letter

parts.note: a trial is a test
XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team

explanation.surface: A cricket side flies off after a Test match ends ahead of schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finished early' cuts TRIAL to TRIA and 'going up' turns it to AIRT. Test suggests cricket's Test matches; XI is an eleven-player side.
explanation.definitionFit: A small chartered aircraft hired for short trips is how a team might fly home.

clue.text: Free at a price — perfidious Albion!

indicators.note: perfidious means treacherous, untrustworthy, so the letters cannot be trusted to stay in order

explanation.surface: A jibe at England: it gives things away only for a fee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfidious Albion' is an old foreign jibe at England's supposed treachery.
explanation.definitionFit: A defendant released pending trial after a sum is pledged is at liberty, but at a cost.

clue.text: With extra drum, get to stop barrel revolving

indicators.note: to stop means plugging a gap, so one piece goes inside the other
revolving means turning round, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a butt is a large barrel for wine or rainwater
to win is to get or gain

explanation.surface: Getting an additional drum stops a barrel from spinning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolving' turns the barrel round and 'to stop' plugs the win inside. A twin tub is an old washing machine with separate washing and spinning drums.
explanation.definitionFit: This washing machine has two drums, one to wash and one to spin, so it has an extra one.

clue.text: Like warm wine?

parts.note: warm means friendly or kind
red is red wine

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone enjoys mulled wine.
explanation.walkthrough: Like is the adjective, similar, not the verb of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindred spirits are alike or related, so the adjective means similar in nature.

clue.text: Drop New Jersey, perhaps, having Luxembourg in mind

indicators.note: in says one piece sits within the other

parts.note: cave! is Latin schoolboy slang for 'beware', that is 'mind out'
L is the international vehicle code for Luxembourg

explanation.surface: Abandon an American state while thinking of a European one.
explanation.walkthrough: New Jersey is a new Jersey cow, a dairy breed, not the US state. Cave (KAY-vee) was British public-school slang for 'look out'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cow giving birth drops its young, and a newborn Jersey calf is the example given.

clue.text: Tax collectors once initially acting with zero authority turned to old emperor

indicators.note: turned means the whole assembly is read backwards

parts.note: IR, the Inland Revenue, was the UK tax office before HMRC

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the next word

parts.note: FA, as in sweet FA, means nothing at all
a tsar is an official with wide powers, as in a drugs tsar

explanation.surface: Former taxmen with no power somehow became an ancient ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned' reverses the whole string. Sweet FA is British slang for nothing. Ras Tafari was Haile Selassie's name before he was crowned Ethiopian emperor.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the pre-coronation name of Haile Selassie, the Ethiopian ruler of the twentieth century.

clue.text: Cake, plonk, something served for exclusive party

definitions.meaning: to cake is to harden or solidify
to plonk something is to put it down heavily
in tennis a player serves for the match or for this unit of play
a clique or social group, as in the jet ___

explanation.surface: A list of food and cheap wine for a private function.
explanation.definitionFit: The word has many senses: to harden, to put down, a tennis division, and a social circle.

clue.text: As theme, effective: revealing lots

parts.note: for means as, in 'taken for granted'
a theme is a tune or melody
telling means effective, striking

explanation.surface: A comment that an essay's subject works well and says a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: Lots means one's fates in life, not 'a great deal'.
explanation.definitionFit: Seers predict a person's destiny, and a lot is one's fate or destiny.
